Become more self sufficient.. 

my husband and i started micro homsteading while also still having our jobs. 
Meaning. We don't just have a cute little garden. We grow our crops internationally. 

Collard greens that we rotate all year round. Blanch and freeze. Turnips, beets, onions and potatoes that we will process and store as well. 

When we bought this house, it didn't check any of our wishlist boxes. But what it did check was its bones were in good shape. And if the market flipped we could still easily afford our mortgage. It was the price that made up buy this small home. We saw People out here also trying to buy to fit their esthetics. And we saw how broke they were.

We live well within city limits. Downtown is literally 4 blocks away. We checked out rules. We can own chickens. Great! So we have 5. We built the coop mostly from stuff we got off Facebook market for free. The rest cost us less than $200. 

Husband hunts. We saved up to buy a budget meat grinder. We now buy meat and fat on sale and make our own sausages. We process our venison and make pastrami and sausages. Among other things. I never pay full price for meat. Literally every. And I will shop at multiple stores to find the deals. 

Ive noticed the more self sufficient we became. The cheaper everything became. Because we spend WAY less. Is it hard work? Absolutely. Is it worth it. Heck yes.

But that's just what's working for us

comments.text:
GenX here. Things are expensive and I'm sick of the fraud, waste and abuse of gov't spending. Our national debt is almost 40 trillion - insane.

However, I also recall I grew up in a 990 sq/ft house. My parents and two sisters with one bathroom. Dad eventually made a room in the musty MI basement for me. He was a blue collar waste water plant worker. Mom largely stayed home to car for us until my youngest sister was in at least middle school. We stayed in that house over 20 years. Dad eventually became #2 at the small plant and retired. My parents saved and were frugal. We borrowed pop up campers to camp for a week in the summer. One year we stayed for free in a friends Florida home over Christmas (actually went to Disney), somehow drove a manual Chevy Citation to FL. It broke there and Dad repaired it. We rarely ate out which was usually getting pizza from the party store on Friday. Mom often dried laundry on a cloths line and we ate a lot of casserole something or other. My Dad retired from his full-time job by 55 and still worked part-time for a few years. He received a pension and took SS at 62. Now at 80 my parents have more in their retirement account than they know what to do with. Oh, and they bought their first house at an interest rate of about 10%.

As much as I hate my current job at 53, I'm there to pay off my mortgage by 56 and help get three kids launched. I retired from law enforcement at 50 and also receive a pension. We lived a used car lifestyle and my kids have never been to Disney, unlike the one big family trip my parents took me and my siblings on. I started building my retiremt account at 25, while my wife worked part-time and we traded the kids as one came home and the other went to work. At this point my retirement account is about 730K and I'll be turning it on at 59.5.

So yep, it's not easy, but how many people today shoot themselves in the foot by doing things out of order. It should be job, marriage, then kids. People also need to live within their means. How many of us buy Starbucks frequently, drive leased vehicles (payments forever), eat out too much, buy our kids crap they don't need, etc. My parents certainly didn't have it easy, but they managed and later thrived by living within their means and saving.
